questions.stem: Which are the three syllabus purposes of data visualisation?
options: Simplifying understanding, telling a story, highlighting significant results
Simplifying understanding, comparing categories, highlighting significant results
Exploring, explaining, persuading
Describing, predicting, prescribing
questions.explanation: Use these exact words in an exam. (C) is a genuine alternative framing used in the literature and (D) is the analytics ladder — both are real, neither is what the syllabus names. Additional purposes worth adding for depth: exploration vs explanation, monitoring KPIs, comparison, forecasting and persuasion.

questions.stem: Pre-attentive attributes are visual properties that:
options: Are perceived with equal accuracy regardless of which attribute is used
Are processed only once the viewer consciously studies the chart
Are processed almost instantly, before conscious attention is directed at them
Are determined by the level of measurement of the data being encoded
questions.explanation: Position, length, size, colour, shape and orientation are perceived in under a quarter of a second. (A) is the trap: they are not equally accurate — position and length are judged far better than angle and area, which is exactly why bar charts beat pie charts.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants to compare total sales across 15 product categories with long names. The best chart is:
options: Pie chart
Vertical column chart
Horizontal bar chart
Treemap
questions.explanation: (B) is right about the encoding but wrong about the orientation — 15 long labels under a vertical axis must be rotated or truncated to fit. (D) would fit the labels but encodes value by area, which is judged far less accurately than length. The axis must start at zero for a length-encoded comparison.

questions.stem: Which chart is most appropriate for showing the relationship between two continuous variables?
options: Histogram
Line chart
Scatter plot
Stacked bar chart
questions.explanation: Scatter plot — (B) is the near-miss: a line chart also plots two continuous axes, but connecting the points asserts an ordered sequence — appropriate for time, misleading for two independent measures. (A) shows the distribution of a single variable. Adding a third variable via marker size makes a scatter a bubble chart.

questions.stem: A histogram differs from a bar chart because it:
options: Encodes frequency using the width of each bar rather than its height
Shows discrete categories grouped into bins, with gaps between the bars
Always begins at zero, whereas a bar chart need not
Shows the distribution of a continuous variable in bins, with no gaps between the bars
questions.explanation: Bar charts compare discrete categories; histograms show the shape of a distribution — skew, spread and bimodality that a single mean conceals. The absence of gaps is the visual signal that the axis is continuous, so the bars are physically adjacent.

questions.stem: A choropleth map of total COVID cases by region is misleading unless the data is:
options: Aggregated into a coarser set of regions to reduce visual noise
Normalised per head of population
Shown with a diverging rather than a sequential colour scale
Restricted to regions that returned a complete dataset
questions.explanation: An un-normalised choropleth mostly maps where people live — the darkest regions are simply the most populous. (A), (C) and (D) are all real cartographic decisions that improve a map without fixing this particular fault. Rates per 100,000 make regions comparable.

questions.stem: Which visualisation best shows part-to-whole composition changing over time?
options: A series of pie charts, one for each period
Stacked area or stacked bar chart
A multi-series line chart, one line per component
A grouped bar chart, one group per period
questions.explanation: (A) is a real practice and a poor one — comparing angles across charts is even harder than within one. (C) shows each component's change but loses the total and the proportions. Stacked area/bar shows both the total and the changing mix, though comparing non-baseline bands across time is genuinely hard for readers.

questions.stem: A box plot is preferred over a bar of means when you want to show:
options: Median, quartiles, spread and outliers
The total value accumulated by each category
The distribution of a single continuous variable across a series of bins
The relationship between two continuous variables
questions.explanation: (C) is the closest — a histogram also shows distribution, but for one variable at a time, whereas box plots are built for comparing distributions across groups. "Bar of means" hides everything about distribution: two groups with identical means can have wildly different spreads and outliers.

questions.stem: The main criticism of pie charts is that:
options: Pie charts cannot be interpreted at all when reproduced in greyscale
Pie charts always understate the largest category relative to the smallest
Pie charts require the underlying data to be at ratio level of measurement
Humans judge angle and area far less accurately than they judge position and length
questions.explanation: This is a claim about human perception, not about the data — which is what (A), (B) and (C) each get wrong by locating the fault elsewhere. Keep to five slices or fewer, order them, label directly — or use a bar chart instead.

questions.stem: Which is the key difference between an infographic and a dashboard?
options: A dashboard is a static, designer-curated narrative; an infographic is dynamic, live and user-filtered
An infographic is a static, designer-curated narrative; a dashboard is dynamic, live and user-filtered
An infographic presents a single metric; a dashboard presents many metrics at once
An infographic is produced for external audiences; a dashboard for internal ones
questions.explanation: (D) describes a common tendency rather than the defining difference — plenty of dashboards are public. Infographic = one story, one audience, one moment. Dashboard = ongoing monitoring, user-driven interrogation, live data. A report is the detailed written analysis with methodology.

questions.stem: A "big number" KPI tile is most effective when it:
options: Is placed at the top-left of the dashboard, where the eye lands first
Is rendered large enough to be legible from across the room
Is shown to full precision, so that no information is lost to rounding
Is paired with a comparison — versus target, versus last period, or a trend sparkline
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) are reasonable presentation advice that do nothing for interpretation. A number without a reference point carries no meaning: "$1.2M" says nothing; "$1.2M, 8% above target, up from $1.05M" says everything.

questions.stem: A word cloud should be described as:
options: A precise comparison of the relative frequency of each term in a corpus
An impressionistic view of term frequency, rather than a quantitative tool
A part-to-whole chart, in which total area represents the whole corpus
A sentiment analysis, in which the most prominent words indicate the dominant mood
questions.explanation: Word size maps to frequency, but layout is arbitrary, long words look bigger than short ones of equal frequency, and context is lost entirely. (D) is the most dangerous misuse — frequency says nothing about valence, so "delay", "refund" and "excellent" all just look big.

questions.stem: Small multiples are preferred over a single multi-series line chart when:
options: There is a single series whose values change sharply over time
There are many series that would overlap into an unreadable "spaghetti chart"
The variables are nominal rather than continuous
The series use different units and therefore cannot share a common axis
questions.explanation: A grid of identically scaled mini-charts preserves comparability while removing overplotting. (D) is exactly backwards — shared axes are essential, and small multiples with independently scaled axes produce a comparison that is visually compelling and completely false.

questions.stem: A Sankey diagram is best used to show:
options: Flow, and the magnitude of that flow, between stages or categories
Correlation between two continuous variables
Hierarchy, with area encoding the size of each nested category
The change in a single value across a sequence of time periods
questions.explanation: Band width encodes volume — ideal for customer journey drop-off, energy flow, or budget allocation across departments. (C) describes a treemap, the other "area encodes size" chart it is most often confused with.

questions.stem: In choosing a chart, the first question to ask is:
options: How much screen or page space is available for the chart?
What question is the audience trying to answer, and what is the data's level of measurement?
Which chart types is this audience already familiar with reading?
Which chart type will make the finding look most compelling?
questions.explanation: (C) is a real and reasonable consideration — just not the first one, since familiarity constrains presentation rather than determining fitness for purpose. (D) is how misleading visuals get made: choosing the chart first and then finding data to fit it.

questions.stem: "Q4 revenue is forecast at $1.8M ± 8%" is an example of which level of analytics?
options: Diagnostic
Descriptive
Predictive
Prescriptive
questions.explanation: Predictive — what will happen. Descriptive = what happened; diagnostic = why it happened; prescriptive = what we should do about it. The verb tense in the statement is usually the fastest tell.

questions.stem: "Shift $40,000 of marketing spend to the underperforming region" is:
options: Diagnostic
Predictive
Prescriptive
Descriptive
questions.explanation: Prescriptive — recommending an action. It sits at the top of the value ladder and demands the highest data quality and model confidence, because a wrong prescription costs money directly rather than merely misinforming.

questions.stem: Most enterprise dashboards stop at descriptive analytics. To climb to predictive, an enterprise most needs:
options: A larger volume of current data, refreshed more frequently than at present
Sufficient clean historical data, reasonably stable underlying conditions, and modelling capability
More sophisticated visualisation software offering forecasting chart types
Broader access to the dashboard, so that more staff can interpret the trends
questions.explanation: (C) is the trap that catches organisations in real life — a trendline drawn by charting software is not a forecast, and it carries no confidence interval. Naming which level a system reaches, and what would be needed to advance one level, is a reliable way to earn marks in an evaluate question.

questions.stem: A repeating pattern of higher sales every December is:
options: Seasonality
A trend
An outlier
A cyclical pattern
questions.explanation: Seasonality — (D) is the fine distinction worth knowing: a cycle also repeats, but over a variable and unpredictable period (like an economic cycle), whereas seasonality has a fixed, known period. Failing to account for it makes December-to-January comparisons meaningless.

questions.stem: Predictive analytics requires all of the following except:
options: Honestly reported confidence intervals
Sufficient clean historical data
Reasonably stable underlying conditions
Guaranteed causal relationships between all of the variables involved
questions.explanation: Useful prediction can rest on stable correlation — you do not need to know why an association holds in order to forecast with it. The caution is that a purely correlational model breaks precisely when the underlying conditions shift, which is why (C) matters so much.

questions.stem: GPUs transformed data analytics primarily because they:
options: Reduce the latency of transfers between storage and the processor
Hold far more data in fast memory than a CPU is able to address
Execute each individual instruction considerably faster than a CPU does
Perform massively parallel matrix computation, enabling deep learning and fast large-scale analysis
questions.explanation: Parallel arithmetic is exactly what neural network training needs. (C) is the reverse of the truth — an individual GPU core is slower than a CPU core, and the advantage comes entirely from having thousands of them working at once. TPUs and NPUs extend the idea; distributed clusters (Hadoop/Spark) scale it horizontally.

questions.stem: The most significant effect of collapsing storage costs on enterprise analytics has been:
options: Enterprises can afford more frequent backups, improving business continuity
Enterprises retain raw historical data instead of aggregating it away, enabling retrospective analysis and ML training
Enterprises can hold entire datasets in memory, removing the disk read bottleneck
Enterprises can retain personal data for longer without breaching retention obligations
questions.explanation: Cheap object storage made "keep everything, decide later" economically rational — which created both the data lake and the data swamp. (D) is the trap: what limits retention of personal data is law and policy, not cost, and cheap storage arguably made over-retention more tempting rather than more permissible.

questions.stem: In-memory processing improves analytics by:
options: Removing the disk read bottleneck, so queries return in seconds rather than minutes
Compressing the dataset so that more of it fits within the available storage
Distributing the query across many machines so each handles a smaller share
Pre-computing common aggregates so they need not be recalculated on each query
questions.explanation: (C) is distributed processing and (D) is a cube or materialised view — three genuinely different techniques for the same symptom, which is what makes them adjacent. The consequence of in-memory processing is behavioural as much as technical: analysis becomes interactive, so an analyst can ask a follow-up question while still holding the thought.

questions.stem: The move from 4G to 5G most directly enables which change in visualisation?
options: Real-time streaming dashboards and mobile decision-making at the point of work
Charts rendered at higher resolution on mobile devices
Larger datasets downloaded to a device for offline analysis
More users able to view the same dashboard at the same time
questions.explanation: (C) and (D) trade only on the bandwidth half of the improvement; the transformative half is low latency, which is what makes a live operational dashboard usable on a factory floor, in a warehouse or in a vehicle.

questions.stem: The democratisation of analytics through self-service BI has which significant downside?
options: The training burden of bringing non-analysts up to a usable standard
The load placed on the warehouse by many concurrent ad-hoc queries
The licensing cost of providing BI tools to every member of staff
"Shadow BI" — proliferating unofficial reports with conflicting numbers and no governance
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (C) are all real costs, but each is a manageable operational one. When everyone can build a dashboard, everyone can build a different answer to the same question — and the organisation loses the ability to say which is right. Governance (certified datasets, agreed measure definitions) is the counterweight.

questions.stem: In an OLAP cube, "sales revenue" is a:
options: Hierarchy
Dimension
Measure, or fact
Attribute
questions.explanation: Measure (fact) — the number being analysed. Time, product, store and customer are dimensions, each of which contains a hierarchy (year → quarter → month) built from attributes. All four terms describe parts of the same cube.

questions.stem: Restricting an OLAP cube to a single value on one dimension (e.g. year = 2026) is:
options: Dice
Slice
Drill-down
Roll-up
questions.explanation: Slice — one dimension fixed, producing a single flat sheet from the cube. The number of dimensions constrained is what separates slice from dice.

questions.stem: Selecting 2026 and NSW/VIC and Laptops from a cube is:
options: Slice
Dice
Pivot
Drill-down
questions.explanation: Dice — constraining several dimensions at once to produce a smaller sub-cube, which is still a cube rather than a flat sheet. Compare with Q127: one constraint slices, several dice.

questions.stem: Moving from Year → Quarter → Month is:
options: Roll-up
Drill-down
Dice
Pivot
questions.explanation: Drill-down — descending a hierarchy to greater detail. The reverse (Month → Quarter → Year) is roll-up, which is (A). Note that neither operation changes which dimensions are included, only the level within one.

questions.stem: Swapping the row and column dimensions to view the same data differently is:
options: Roll-up
Slice
Dice
Pivot
questions.explanation: Pivot (rotate) — Same data, same level of detail, new perspective — the operation that gives pivot tables their name. Nothing is filtered and nothing is aggregated differently, which is what distinguishes it from the other three.

questions.stem: MOLAP compared with ROLAP:
options: MOLAP pre-aggregates into a cube, giving the fastest queries but heavier storage and refresh lag
MOLAP queries the relational warehouse directly, handling larger datasets but responding more slowly
MOLAP stores only the dimensions, with the measures queried live from the warehouse
MOLAP and ROLAP differ only in the query language used to interrogate them
questions.explanation: (B) is ROLAP described as though it were MOLAP, and (C) is roughly HOLAP, the genuine hybrid — pre-aggregate the hot summaries, query the detail live. ROLAP handles larger data with slower response; MOLAP trades storage and freshness for speed.

questions.stem: A star schema consists of:
options: A set of dimension tables with no central fact table
A central fact table surrounded by dimension tables that are themselves normalised
A chain of fully normalised tables linked by foreign keys
A central fact table surrounded by denormalised dimension tables
questions.explanation: Deliberately denormalised for query speed and simplicity. (B) is a snowflake schema — the same structure with the dimensions normalised further, giving less redundancy but more joins and slower queries.

questions.stem: Which best describes the difference between OLTP and OLAP workloads?
options: OLTP is denormalised for speed; OLAP is normalised for integrity
OLTP handles few large complex reads; OLAP handles many small writes
OLTP handles many small writes to run the business; OLAP handles few large complex reads to analyse it
OLTP stores years of history; OLAP stores only the current position
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (D) each state a true fact about the pair with the two systems swapped. OLTP: current, detailed, normalised, millisecond response, integrity-focused. OLAP: historical, aggregated, denormalised, seconds-to-minutes, query-speed-focused.

questions.stem: Pre-aggregation in an OLAP layer matters for visualisation because:
options: A dashboard can respond instantly to drill-down, making the visualisation exploratory rather than a static picture
The dataset shrinks enough to be embedded directly within the dashboard file
Aggregation removes outliers, so the resulting charts are less distorted by extreme values
Aggregated values are inherently cleaner, reducing the need for validation before charting
questions.explanation: (C) is quietly dangerous — aggregation conceals outliers rather than removing them, which is a reason for caution, not a benefit. Responsiveness changes the kind of thinking a user can do: sub-second answers support a chain of follow-up questions; thirty-second answers do not.

questions.stem: A key limitation of relying on a data warehouse for a real-time operations dashboard is:
options: ETL discards the underlying records once they have been aggregated
Refresh latency means the warehouse may be hours behind live operations
Warehouse schemas are normalised, so operational queries require too many joins
A warehouse holds data from only one source system, so operational context is missing
questions.explanation: (C) and (D) are the reverse of a warehouse's defining properties — it is deliberately denormalised and integrated from many sources. Operational monitoring needs a streaming or direct-query path; the warehouse is for integrated historical analysis, and many enterprises run both.

questions.stem: Data warehousing supports visualisation of historical trends primarily because it:
options: Retains years of integrated, conformed history, so long-run trend and year-on-year comparison are possible
Stores only the most recent period, so every chart reflects current performance
Compresses older records, so a longer history fits within the same storage
Refreshes continuously, so historical values are updated as corrections arrive
questions.explanation: "One version of the truth" — every department's chart uses the same definition of the same measure across the same history. (D) contradicts a defining property: a warehouse is non-volatile, so history does not change under you, which is what makes trend comparison trustworthy.

questions.stem: A hidden risk of ETL for the person reading a dashboard is that:
options: Cleaning and transformation decisions made in the pipeline are invisible in the final chart
The load schedule introduces a delay, so the chart may show yesterday's position
ETL creates a second copy of the data, which can diverge from the source system
ETL aggregates the data, so the chart cannot be drilled down to individual records
questions.explanation: All four are genuine consequences of ETL — the word in the stem is hidden. Latency, duplication and grain are all knowable from the dashboard's documentation, whereas rows excluded, nulls imputed and categories merged during Transform never appear on the visual at all. This is why provenance and methodology notes belong on serious dashboards.

questions.stem: The four syllabus criteria for data integrity in developing a visualisation are:
options: Relevance, accuracy, validity, reliability
Ownership, source, validation, risk
Ownership, accuracy, validation, risk
Ownership, source, verification, risk
questions.explanation: Ownership, source, validation, risk — (C) and (D) each substitute a single plausible word, and (A) is RAVR — used for assessing data rather than the visualisation development process. Build every "assess data integrity" answer on these four.

questions.stem: In the integrity criterion ownership, the key question is:
options: Who produced the visualisation and is accountable for its conclusions?
Which team within the enterprise is accountable for the quality of the data?
Which system of record holds the authoritative copy of the data?
Who owns or licenses the data, and do you have the right to use and republish it?
questions.explanation: (B) is data stewardship and (C) is the system of record — both are real governance concepts that share the vocabulary of ownership. This criterion is about rights: contractual restrictions, third-party licensing and ICIP obligations for Indigenous data. Permission to analyse is not automatically permission to publish.

questions.stem: A visualisation is built from a dataset whose schema silently changed at source. This is a failure of:
options: Ongoing validation and change monitoring
Ownership, since nobody was accountable for the source data
Risk, since the dependency on that source was never assessed
Chart selection, since the chart type no longer suits the data
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) are the sibling integrity criteria and both are arguably implicated — but validation is the control that detects the change, which is what failed here. A silently renamed or re-typed field produces a chart that still renders and is now wrong: the most dangerous class of error, because nothing looks broken.

questions.stem: Poor data quality most directly limits:
options: The scope of visible information and the depth of insight achievable
The range of chart types available to the developer
The frequency at which the dashboard can be refreshed
The number of users who can be granted access to the dashboard
questions.explanation: Sparse or noisy data forces fewer segments, shorter timeframes and higher aggregation — capping the work at descriptive insight with wide error bars, and putting predictive analytics out of reach entirely.

questions.stem: "Defensive design" in response to low-quality data means:
options: Omitting the least reliable series entirely, so that no misleading conclusion can be drawn from it
Restricting access so that only users who understand the limitations can view the dashboard
Aggregating to a higher level, so the noisy underlying values are never exposed
Showing ranges rather than point estimates, annotating caveats, and displaying sample sizes and collection dates
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (C) are all real responses, and all three hide the problem rather than disclosing it — which is the opposite of the intent. Honesty about uncertainty is a design decision: a confident-looking point estimate on shaky data is a misleading visualisation even when every number in it is technically correct.

questions.stem: The syllabus's four lenses on bias in visualisation are:
options: Accuracy, audience, data source, selection bias
Accuracy, audience, data source, unconscious bias
Ownership, audience, data source, unconscious bias
Accuracy, aggregation, data source, unconscious bias
questions.explanation: Accuracy (errors and systematic omissions), audience (designing to please), data source (a single source or a shared blind spot) and unconscious bias (the developer's own assumptions). Each distractor swaps in a term that is real but belongs to a different framework.

questions.stem: Bias introduced at the collection stage:
options: Affects the analysis but not the visualisation, which merely displays the result
Is largely removed by the cleaning and transformation steps of ETL
Can be corrected by statistically weighting the sample during analysis
Persists and typically compounds through storage, analysis and visualisation
questions.explanation: (C) is the honest near-miss: weighting genuinely helps where you know which groups were under-sampled and by how much — it cannot recover the views of people who were never approached. "Bias is never removed by a later stage, only amplified" is the sentence to write in a 6–8 mark question.

questions.stem: A column chart whose y-axis starts at 95 rather than 0 is misleading because:
options: Bars encode value by position, so the baseline is irrelevant to how they are read
Bars encode value by length, so truncating the baseline exaggerates small differences
A truncated axis compresses the differences, understating genuine change
A truncated axis makes the chart impossible to compare against any other chart
questions.explanation: (C) states the effect backwards. The encoding is the reason: because bars are read by length, the bar must begin at zero or its length no longer represents the value. Line charts, which encode by position and emphasise change, may legitimately use a truncated axis if it is clearly labelled.

questions.stem: Dual y-axes with independently chosen scales are dangerous because they:
options: Require both series to share the same unit of measurement to be valid
Cannot be labelled clearly enough for a reader to tell which series belongs to which axis
Can be scaled to manufacture the appearance of correlation between unrelated series
Prevent the chart from being drilled down to a lower level of detail
questions.explanation: The crossing point and the apparent tracking are artefacts of the scales chosen, not properties of the data — slide one axis and the "relationship" appears or vanishes. Indexing both series to a common base (say, 100 at the start) is the honest alternative.

questions.stem: Scaling a circle's radius rather than its area to a value:
options: Exaggerates small values, because a minimum radius must be enforced for visibility
Substantially understates large values, because area grows more slowly than the radius
Has no perceptual effect, since readers compare the widest dimension of each circle
Substantially exaggerates large values, because area grows with the square of the radius
questions.explanation: Doubling the radius quadruples the perceived area, so a value twice as large looks four times as large. Bubble charts must encode value by area — most charting software does this correctly by default, which is precisely why hand-built graphics get it wrong.

questions.stem: In a stimulus question, a chart shows sales rising from a start date chosen just after a slump. The technique is:
options: Aggregation to a coarser period
A cherry-picked timeframe
Normalisation against a baseline
A truncated axis
questions.explanation: Selecting the baseline that flatters the conclusion. (A) and (D) are the other two ways of achieving a similar effect, which is why they are plausible here — but the manipulation described is specifically of the start point. The counter is to show the full available series, or to annotate why that start point is analytically meaningful.

questions.stem: Which is the most invisible form of editorial control in a visualisation?
options: The level of aggregation at which the data is displayed
The chart title, which frames how the reader interprets what follows
The colour scale, which directs the eye toward particular values
Filtering — what has been included and what has been excluded
questions.explanation: All four are genuine editorial choices, and (A), (B) and (C) are all on the page — the title can be read, the scale can be seen, and the axis labels usually reveal the grain. Readers cannot see the records that were silently dropped. Always ask what the filter set is and whether nulls were excluded.

questions.stem: A trend visible in every subgroup reverses when the subgroups are combined. This is:
options: Simpson's paradox
Selection bias
Seasonality
Regression to the mean
questions.explanation: Simpson's paradox — an aggregation effect driven by differing subgroup sizes. It is the strongest argument for asking what level of aggregation a chart uses before believing its conclusion, since both the aggregated and disaggregated figures are arithmetically correct.

questions.stem: For a 40-million-row dataset requiring live refresh and role-based access, the most appropriate tool category is:
options: A scheduled report exported to PDF and distributed by email
A spreadsheet dashboard built on a live database connection
Business analytics as a service (Power BI, Tableau)
A static infographic refreshed each quarter by a designer
questions.explanation: (B) is the closest — a live connection solves the refresh requirement, but spreadsheets still fail past roughly a million rows and offer no row-level security. The BI tool's costs — licensing, learning curve, data sovereignty — are the balancing points to name in an evaluate question.

questions.stem: The chief weakness of presenting data via presentation software is:
options: It cannot render the chart types enterprise reporting requires
It is a static snapshot — out of date the moment it is exported, and it cannot be interrogated
It cannot connect to a live data source under any circumstances
It gives the author no control over the order in which findings are presented
questions.explanation: (C) is the near-miss: modern presentation software can link to live data, but the deck that gets emailed round is still a snapshot, and nobody receiving it can filter or drill. Its strengths are narrative control — which disposes of (D) — and universal familiarity, which is why it remains right for a one-off executive briefing.

questions.stem: A custom-coded visualisation (for example in D3.js) is best justified when:
options: A novel or bespoke visual form is required for a public-facing product that off-the-shelf tools cannot produce
The dataset is too large for a BI tool to render within an acceptable response time
The organisation wants to avoid the recurring licence cost of a commercial BI tool
The visualisation must be embedded within an existing web application
questions.explanation: (C) and (D) are real motivations that do not survive scrutiny — embedding is a standard BI feature, and the development and maintenance cost of custom code dwarfs any licence saving. You are buying unlimited flexibility, and paying with development cost, timeline, maintenance liability and an accessibility burden a BI tool would have handled for you.

questions.stem: Which is a genuine risk of spreadsheet dashboards in an enterprise?
options: Spreadsheets cannot connect to a database, so all data must be pasted in manually
Version sprawl — multiple conflicting copies with no single source of truth
Spreadsheets cannot apply conditional formatting or provide interactive filters
Spreadsheets cannot be opened by more than one person at the same time
questions.explanation: "Which file is current?" is the archetypal spreadsheet governance failure, alongside manual refresh and fragile cross-workbook links. (A), (C) and (D) all understate what modern spreadsheets can do — the problem is governance, not capability.

questions.stem: When justifying a visualisation tool in an exam, the strongest structure is:
options: Identify the tool most widely used in the industry and justify the choice by precedent
Compare the licensing and training cost of each option over three years and select the lowest
Describe the capabilities of each candidate tool in equal detail, then state a preference
State explicit criteria (data volume, interactivity, audience skill, update frequency, cost, security, scalability), evaluate the options against them, and say why the alternatives are worse
questions.explanation: "Justify" demands argument, evidence, and explicit rejection of the alternatives. (B) is a real analysis that silently drops every non-financial criterion; feature lists and precedent cap out at half marks.

questions.stem: The five syllabus moves for interrogating a visualisation are:
options: Slice, dice, drill-down, roll-up, pivot
Interpret, aggregation, filtering, outliers, evaluation
Ownership, source, validation, risk, cost
Interpret, aggregation, filtering, outliers, reasoning
questions.explanation: (B) substitutes a single word that sounds entirely at home. Use these five as the structure for any stimulus question — they are effectively a mark scheme in disguise.

questions.stem: When first interrogating a visualisation, you should read:
options: The caption's stated conclusion, then check whether the chart supports it
The shape of the data first, then the labels that explain it
Title, axes, units, scale, legend, source and date — before interpreting the shape
The source and date first, since these determine whether the chart is worth reading at all
questions.explanation: (D) is a sophisticated partial answer — provenance matters, but reading it alone still leaves you interpreting a shape without knowing its scale. Reading the shape first, as in (B), is exactly how a truncated axis fools people.

questions.stem: A single extreme outlier in a scatter plot can:
options: Drag the mean, stretch the axis, and create or destroy an apparent trend
Shift the mean, while leaving the axis range and the apparent trend unchanged
Shift the median, while leaving the mean and the trend line unaffected
Be disregarded, since one point cannot alter a trend drawn across many observations
questions.explanation: The axis-stretching effect is the one most often missed: a single distant point rescales the whole plot and compresses every other observation into a corner. Report the median alongside the mean, show the distribution, and state whether the outlier is an error or a genuine and important extreme.

questions.stem: Which title is the strongest for a dashboard chart?
options: "Sales by month, with the July price rise annotated"
"Monthly sales, January–December 2026"
"Sales fell 12% after the July price rise"
"Impact of the July price rise on sales"
questions.explanation: (A) and (D) are both perfectly respectable topic titles — they tell you what the chart is about, but leave the reader to work out what it shows and risk each reader reaching a different conclusion. An insight-led title states the finding.

questions.stem: The difference between UX and UI is:
options: UX covers research and testing; UI covers everything that happens after launch
UI is the whole quality of the interaction; UX is the visual and interactive surface, one part of UI
UX is the whole quality of the interaction — usefulness, findability, credibility, accessibility; UI is the visual and interactive surface, one part of UX
UX applies to the dashboard's content; UI applies to the software it is built in
questions.explanation: (B) is the containment relationship inverted, which is the most common error. A beautiful UI on a dashboard in which nobody can find the answer is a UX failure.

questions.stem: Nielsen's heuristic "visibility of system status" applied to a dashboard means:
options: Showing the user which permissions their account currently holds
Showing the company logo and dashboard name in a fixed header
Showing each KPI in red, amber or green according to its performance
Showing loading indicators and a "last refreshed at" timestamp
questions.explanation: The heuristic is about the system telling the user what it is doing. (C) reports on the business, not the system. A dashboard that silently serves stale data because a feed failed overnight is worse than one that shows no data at all.

questions.stem: Which Gestalt principle explains why items placed close together are read as a group?
options: Similarity
Proximity
Enclosure
Continuity
questions.explanation: Proximity — Similarity groups by shared colour or shape; enclosure groups by a shared boundary; continuity leads the eye along a line. Use them deliberately to structure a dashboard through white space rather than by drawing borders everywhere.

questions.stem: Tufte's data-ink ratio principle recommends:
options: Maximising the proportion of ink devoted to data, and removing chartjunk
Minimising the total amount of ink used, so the chart prints economically
Using a consistent ink weight across every element of the chart
Keeping the ratio of chart area to surrounding white space within defined limits
questions.explanation: (B) is the trap: it is a ratio, not a minimum — removing data to use less ink defeats the point entirely. Chartjunk means heavy gridlines, 3-D effects, drop shadows, decorative backgrounds and redundant legends; every element removed makes the remaining data easier to see.

questions.stem: WCAG AA requires a contrast ratio of at least what for normal-size text?
questions.explanation: 4.5:1 — for normal text at AA. (B) is the AA threshold for large text and non-text elements, and (C) is the AAA threshold for normal text — all three are real numbers from the same standard. Also: never rely on colour alone, provide alt text and a data-table alternative, and ensure keyboard navigability.

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of males have some form of colour vision deficiency, and what design rule follows?
options: About 1% — provide a greyscale alternative version of each chart on request
About 8% — use a red/green palette, which those affected perceive as differing in lightness
About 8% — never encode meaning by colour alone; add labels, patterns or direct annotation
About 25% — restrict all charts to a single hue with varying lightness
questions.explanation: (B) carries the correct statistic and the wrong conclusion, which makes it the option to be most careful with: red/green is precisely the pairing that deuteranopia and protanopia collapse. Use colour-blind-safe palettes and encode redundantly with position, shape or direct labels.

questions.stem: Placing the most important KPI at the top-left of a dashboard is justified by:
options: WCAG requirements governing the reading order used by assistive technology
The Gestalt principle of proximity, which groups nearby elements together
Tufte's data-ink ratio, which gives priority to the densest element
F- and Z-pattern scanning behaviour in left-to-right reading cultures
questions.explanation: Eye-tracking shows readers enter at the top-left and scan in F or Z patterns, so screen position is itself a hierarchy decision. (A) is a genuinely tempting invention — WCAG does care about reading order, but it constrains the DOM sequence, not which metric is most important.

questions.stem: Responsive design for a dashboard requires:
options: Fixing element widths in pixels, so the layout is identical on every device
Scaling the desktop layout down proportionally so that it fits the smaller viewport
Reflowing the layout, reducing the number of elements per screen, and using touch targets of at least about 44px
Removing interactivity on mobile, since touch input cannot support filtering
questions.explanation: (B) is the most common misunderstanding — proportional scaling produces a desktop dashboard rendered at unreadable size, which is exactly what responsive design exists to avoid. Mobile layouts should prioritise the two or three metrics that actually drive a decision in the field.

questions.stem: Which is a measurable UX evaluation criterion?
options: "The dashboard follows the organisation's design system and brand palette"
"Users report that the dashboard is clear and easy to navigate"
"Time to find a specified figure ≤ 30 seconds; task completion rate ≥ 90%; SUS score ≥ 68"
"The dashboard contains no more than seven visual elements per screen"
questions.explanation: (D) is the interesting distractor: it is perfectly measurable, but it measures conformance to a design rule, not whether users succeed. Criteria must be defined before testing and must be about user outcomes; vague aesthetic goals can only be asserted, never evaluated.

questions.stem: The best method to discover why users cannot find a figure on a dashboard is:
options: A post-use satisfaction survey asking users to rate findability
Usability testing with a think-aloud protocol
Analytics showing which panels are viewed and for how long
A heuristic review by a designer against Nielsen's principles
questions.explanation: (C) and (D) are both legitimate methods, but analytics tell you that users failed and a heuristic review tells you what a designer predicts will fail. Think-aloud reveals the reasoning behind the actual failure, in the actual user's words.

questions.stem: In the visualisation development workflow, discovering at the exploration stage that a field is 40% null should send you:
options: Back to sourcing and preparing the data
Forward to design, with that field excluded from the visualisation
Forward to testing, to establish whether users notice the gap
Back to defining the question, since this data cannot answer it
questions.explanation: (B) and (D) are both premature: you do not yet know whether the nulls are recoverable, systematic, or an artefact of the extract. The workflow is explicitly iterative — the loops back from exploration to sourcing, and from testing to design, are the point of the diagram.

questions.stem: When incorporating a forecast into a visualisation, best practice is to:
options: Omit the forecast, since modelled values do not belong on a chart of measured data
Show the forecast in the same style as the actuals, with a note in the caption explaining the method
Show only the forecast's end point, labelled with its predicted value
Show the forecast as a visually distinct series with a confidence band, clearly separated from the actuals
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) are the two failure modes — presenting modelled values as if they were measured, and refusing to show the most decision-relevant part of the picture. Visual distinction plus an uncertainty band is the honest treatment.

questions.stem: Row-level security in a BI tool means:
options: Rows are ordered so that the most sensitive records appear last
Each row of the dataset is encrypted separately, with its own key
Users see only the rows they are entitled to see — for example, only their own region's data
Each row records which user last modified it, and when
questions.explanation: One dashboard, many audiences, enforced at the data layer — far safer than maintaining separate filtered copies per team, which reintroduces version sprawl. (D) is an audit trail, which supports accountability rather than access control.

questions.stem: Before publishing an aggregated public dashboard of health data, you should:
options: Publish only national totals, with no geographic breakdown at all
Remove the date labels, so the timing of individual cases cannot be inferred
Round every value to the nearest ten, so no exact count is disclosed
Suppress small cells that could allow individuals to be re-identified
questions.explanation: (C) is the near-miss worth understanding — rounding does not reliably prevent re-identification, because a rounded small cell still reveals that someone in that cohort exists. (A) is safe and useless. A cell reading "1 case, postcode 2170, aged 15–19" is identifying; small-cell suppression and aggregation thresholds are the standard practice.

questions.stem: The best reason to keep the raw data file untouched and clean a separate copy is:
options: Reproducibility — cleaning decisions can be re-examined, reversed or corrected against the original
Storage is inexpensive, so there is no reason to overwrite the original file
The raw file then serves as a backup should the cleaned file be lost or corrupted
Regulators require the original form of any dataset used in reporting to be retained
questions.explanation: (C) is a genuine secondary benefit — but a backup protects against loss, while the reason that matters here is protecting against undetectable error. Once you overwrite the raw file, every downstream mistake becomes permanent and unauditable.

questions.stem: Natural-language query ("show sales by region last quarter") in a BI tool primarily improves:
options: The consistency of measure definitions across the organisation
The accuracy of results, since the system resolves ambiguity in the question itself
The speed at which large queries execute against the warehouse
The accessibility of analysis for non-technical users
questions.explanation: It lowers the skill barrier — with the corresponding risk that a user receives a confident-looking answer to a question the system misinterpreted, which is why (B) is close to backwards.

questions.stem: A dashboard shows a KPI in red. A colour-blind user cannot distinguish it. The most appropriate fix is:
options: Replace the colour coding with an arrow showing the direction of change
Change the red to a colour with a higher contrast ratio against the background
Increase the font size of the KPI so that it is easier to read
Add a redundant cue — an icon, a label, or explicit "below target" text
questions.explanation: (B) treats a hue discrimination problem as a contrast problem, and higher contrast does not make red distinguishable from green. (A) is closer but substitutes direction for status — a metric can be improving and still be below target. Never rely on colour alone; redundant encoding preserves the meaning for everyone while keeping the visual cue for those who can see it.

questions.stem: An executive asks for "everything on one page". The best UX response is:
options: Present the 40 charts as a single scrolling page, ordered by importance
Include all 40 charts at reduced size, so that nothing is omitted
Group the 40 charts into tabs on a single dashboard, keeping everything one click away
Show the three decision-critical KPIs with trend, and provide drill-through to the detail
questions.explanation: (A) and (C) both look like compromises but simply relocate the overload. An executive needs to know whether to act, not to see every measure — and drill-through preserves access to the detail without paying for it in cognitive load.

questions.stem: A visualisation shows total complaints falling while complaints per 1,000 customers are rising. The correct interpretation is:
options: This is Simpson's paradox, since the direction reverses on aggregation
The two series must be drawn from different populations, so one of them is in error
The customer base shrank; the rate is the more meaningful measure of service quality
The per-customer rate is less reliable, since it depends on an estimated denominator
questions.explanation: (A) is the sharpest trap — Simpson's paradox involves subgroups reversing when combined, whereas this is a single population with a shrinking denominator. Normalisation changes the story, and raw counts across a changing denominator are the classic comparison error.

questions.stem: A dashboard's "last updated" timestamp reads three days old, but the data feed actually failed a week ago. The design failure is:
options: The system does not degrade gracefully or surface feed failures to the user
The refresh schedule is too infrequent for the decisions the dashboard supports
The timestamp is presented in a format that users are likely to misread
The dashboard caches its results, so users see a copy rather than a live query
questions.explanation: The specific fault is that the timestamp reports the last successful render, not the last successful load — so the dashboard is confidently lying. Live analysis carries an obligation to show data health; a silently stale dashboard actively misleads decision-makers who believe it is current.

questions.stem: In evaluating a completed dashboard against criteria, the strongest answer structure is:
options: Compare the dashboard against a competitor's and identify where it falls short
Describe each chart in turn, then summarise the dashboard's overall quality
State the criterion → state the evidence or measurement → make a judgement → note the limitation → recommend an improvement
Report the usability testing results in full, then draw a conclusion from them
questions.explanation: (D) is the near-miss worth noticing: evidence without a stated criterion is a report, not an evaluation — you cannot judge a result without saying what would have counted as good. Description alone, as in (B), is a band-3 answer.

questions.stem: Blending live operational data with warehouse history on one dashboard enables:
options: Elimination of the ETL refresh lag that would otherwise delay the warehouse data
Comparison of today's performance against the historical baseline, flagging deviation in real time
A reduction in warehouse storage, since live data need no longer be retained
Automatic reconciliation of any differences between the two data sources
questions.explanation: "Today versus the same day last year" is only possible because the warehouse retains conformed history alongside the live feed. (A) misunderstands the architecture — blending does not remove the lag, it simply routes around it for the series that need to be current.

questions.stem: A council publishes a choropleth of "reported graffiti incidents" per suburb. A significant interpretive caution is:
options: It maps reporting behaviour as much as incidence — suburbs with engaged residents report more
It maps population density, unless the counts are normalised per resident
Suburb boundaries vary in physical size, so larger suburbs draw more visual attention
Reported incidents are ordinal data and so cannot be shown on a continuous colour scale
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) are both real and important choropleth cautions — but they are presentation problems with known fixes, whereas (A) is a flaw in what the data can mean at all. Passive-collection datasets record the act of reporting, not the underlying phenomenon: measurement bias at collection, carried straight into the visual.

questions.stem: A retailer wants a dashboard used by store managers on the shop floor. The most important design decision is:
options: A mobile-responsive layout with few, decision-relevant metrics and large touch targets
Maximum data density, so managers never need to navigate away to find detail
A read-only view, so that store data cannot be altered from the floor
A high-contrast palette, so the screen stays legible under variable store lighting
questions.explanation: Design follows the persona and the context of use — standing, glancing, one-handed on a phone, mid-shift, with thirty seconds to decide something. (C) and (D) are both sensible and both secondary.

questions.stem: Which sequence is the most coherent pipeline for a recurring forecast dashboard?
options: SQL database → Power BI dashboard → exported spreadsheet → forecasting model
Spreadsheet → screenshot → slide deck → emailed PDF
SQL database → Power Query ETL → forecasting model → Power BI dashboard
Forecasting model → SQL database → Power Query ETL → Power BI dashboard
questions.explanation: (A) and (D) contain sensible components in an order that breaks the pipeline — in (A) the forecast is produced after the dashboard that is meant to display it, and in (D) the model runs on data that has not yet been cleaned. Each tool should do what it is best at; the cost is integration complexity and more points of failure.

questions.stem: A visualisation is accurate, attractive and unused. In an evaluation this should be judged:
options: Outside the scope of evaluation, since adoption depends on organisational factors
A success, since both the accuracy and the accessibility criteria were met
A failure against the criterion of communicating to the audience — an unused visualisation delivers no value
A partial success, to be judged properly only once usage has had time to build
questions.explanation: (A) is the sophisticated dodge — organisational factors certainly affect adoption, but a visualisation that does not fit how people work has failed a design criterion, not merely an environmental one. Effectiveness is measured by whether it supports a decision; adoption, task success and acted-on insights are legitimate evaluation criteria.

questions.stem: The main visualisation argument for normalising to an index (e.g. base year = 100) is:
options: It converts the data from interval to ratio level of measurement
It removes the effect of outliers on the shape of each series
It makes series of very different magnitudes comparable in terms of relative change
It adjusts each series for seasonality against its own base period
questions.explanation: (D) is a plausible-sounding invention — indexing rebases, it does not deseasonalise, and a seasonal pattern remains perfectly visible in an indexed series. Indexing is also the honest alternative to a dual-axis chart, which manufactures apparent correlation through arbitrary scaling.

questions.stem: A dashboard designer adds 12 filters "for flexibility". The likely UX consequence is:
options: Choice overload and inconsistent results between users; better to give sensible defaults with fewer, meaningful filters
Slower load times, since each filter adds a query against the underlying dataset
Reduced accessibility, since each filter adds another control to keyboard navigation
Improved task completion, since every user can construct precisely the view they need
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) are real secondary effects, but neither is the primary consequence: the damage is that two people answer the same question differently because they filtered differently. Defaults are a design decision — most users never change them, so the default view is the product.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest evidence that a visualisation improved a business outcome?
options: Positive feedback from stakeholders at a post-launch review
A high and sustained number of views by the intended audience
A measured change in the KPI the visualisation was designed to influence, against a baseline or control
A high task completion rate observed in usability testing
questions.explanation: (D) is the strongest distractor — it is rigorous, measured evidence, but of usability, not of business effect. Outcome evidence beats output evidence: views measure attention, task success measures comprehension, and only the KPI measures effect.

questions.stem: An analyst presents a correlation of 0.85 as proof that advertising drives sales. The best critique is:
options: Correlation does not establish causation — reverse causation and confounders such as seasonality, price changes and competitor activity must be excluded
A correlation of 0.85 is too weak to support any conclusion about a relationship
Correlation cannot be computed on data that has been aggregated into monthly totals
The relationship may not be linear, in which case the coefficient understates its strength
questions.explanation: (D) is a genuine statistical caution and worth knowing — but it would strengthen the analyst's case rather than undermine it. Advertising spend often follows expected demand, which makes reverse causation entirely plausible here. Controlled experiments or A/B tests are what establish causality.

questions.stem: Which visualisation decision most improves credibility with a sceptical audience?
options: Citing the source, collection date, sample size and methodology directly on the visual
Using a restrained, professional palette consistent with the organisation's brand
Stating the conclusion in an insight-led title, so there is no ambiguity about the finding
Including a confidence band around every estimated or modelled value
questions.explanation: (D) is excellent practice and comes a close second — but it only helps where values are modelled, whereas provenance answers the very first question a sceptic asks of any chart: "where did this come from?" Note (C) can actually reduce credibility with a hostile audience, since a stated conclusion reads as advocacy.

questions.stem: A live streaming dashboard refreshing every second, for a metric that changes monthly, is:
options: A minor inefficiency, since the cost of one additional query is negligible
Good design, since more frequent refresh can never make the displayed data less accurate
Necessary for data integrity, since otherwise stale values would be displayed
Poor design — refresh frequency should match the decision cadence, and over-refreshing adds cost and cognitive noise
questions.explanation: (A) is the tempting dismissal: one query is cheap, but one query per second per user is not, and a value that visibly flickers trains users to distrust it. Refresh rate is a design decision balancing decision timeliness against infrastructure cost and user distraction.

questions.stem: In a stimulus question showing a chart with no y-axis label, the correct first observation is:
options: The chart type must be inappropriate, since every chart type requires a labelled axis
Without units and scale, the magnitude of the change cannot be judged, so no conclusion about significance can be drawn
The underlying data must be qualitative, since qualitative data carries no units
The chart is unusable, so no observation at all can be made from it
questions.explanation: (D) overstates it — you can still read the shape, the direction and the ordering; what you cannot judge is magnitude. Missing units is one of the listed misleading techniques, and saying precisely what cannot be concluded is the analytical move markers reward.

questions.stem: An enterprise reports "conversions up 300%". The most important missing context is:
options: The statistical significance of the increase, given the sample size
The definition of "conversion" the enterprise is using
The base — 300% of what absolute number, and across what timeframe
Whether the comparison period was seasonally comparable
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (D) are all genuinely important, which is what makes this hard — but without the base you cannot even tell whether the other three matter. Percentages without a base are a classic misleading technique: 1 → 4 conversions is a 300% increase and commercially meaningless.

questions.stem: VR/AR data environments are most defensible in an enterprise when:
options: The dataset has more dimensions than a two-dimensional chart can encode at once
Spatial context genuinely adds meaning — for example AR overlays of sensor data on a factory floor
The audience is unfamiliar with conventional charts and needs a more intuitive form
The organisation wants to signal technical sophistication to clients and investors
questions.explanation: (A) is the seriously tempting technical argument, and it is wrong for a well-established reason: adding a spatial dimension makes values harder to compare, not easier, because 3-D positions are judged far less accurately than 2-D ones. Novelty is not a justification — the test is whether immersion improves the decision.

questions.stem: The strongest reason to run an accessibility audit before deploying a public dashboard is:
options: Accessible designs generally test better with all users, improving overall usability
Legal compliance obligations, and the exclusion of users who otherwise cannot access public information
Remediation after launch costs considerably more than designing to WCAG from the start
It surfaces contrast problems that also affect users on low-quality or glare-affected displays
questions.explanation: (A) and (C) are both true and are the arguments usually reached for in a business case — but they are incidental benefits. The strongest reason is that inaccessible public information excludes people from a service they are entitled to, and that this is a legal as well as an ethical obligation.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of using visualisation for exploration rather than explanation?
options: An interactive dashboard letting managers filter down to their own region
A polished infographic prepared for a media release
A one-page executive summary of the quarter's results
An analyst cross-filtering a scatter matrix to discover which variables relate, before forming a hypothesis
questions.explanation: (A) is the trap — interactivity is not exploration. A filterable dashboard answers questions the designer anticipated; exploration is analyst-facing, fast, ugly and iterative, and its purpose is to find the question. Confusing the two produces cluttered dashboards and shallow reports.

questions.stem: A dashboard aggregates results to the national level and a regional manager complains it is useless. The best design response is:
options: Add drill-down and role-based default filters, so each user lands on their own region with the ability to roll up
Build a separate dashboard for each region, so every manager sees only their own data
Change the default aggregation to regional and let national users roll up instead
Add a region filter, and instruct managers to select their own region each time they open it
questions.explanation: (B) reintroduces version sprawl across thirty artefacts, (C) simply moves the problem to the national users, and (D) ignores that most users never change a default. One well-modelled dataset with drill-down and row-level security serves many personas from a single source of truth.

questions.stem: In an 8-mark question on bias in a visualisation, the strongest structure names:
options: The stage at which bias entered and a mitigation for each instance found in the stimulus
Each of the four bias lenses, defined and illustrated with an example drawn from the stimulus
The stage at which bias entered, the mechanism, its effect on the conclusion, and a mitigation — with a judgement
The misleading design techniques present in the visual, each identified and corrected
questions.explanation: (A) is very close and would score well — what it omits is the effect on the conclusion, which is the step that converts identification into analysis. Naming the stage and the mechanism demonstrates analysis rather than description, and gives a natural four-paragraph structure.

questions.stem: Which is the most defensible criterion set for evaluating a completed enterprise dashboard?
options: Task completion rate, time to insight, adoption, and a stakeholder satisfaction score
Accuracy against source, appropriateness of chart type, colour accessibility, and consistency with the brand palette
Accuracy against source, task completion rate, time to insight, accessibility conformance, adoption, and measured effect on the target KPI
Accuracy against source, refresh reliability, query performance, and infrastructure cost
questions.explanation: (B) is a design review, (A) omits accuracy entirely — a fast, well-adopted dashboard showing wrong numbers is the worst outcome of all — and (D) is an operations review. Only (C) spans correctness, usability, inclusion and business effect. State the criteria explicitly before evaluating against them.

questions.stem: The single most important thing a visualisation developer can do to protect data integrity is:
options: Apply validation rules to the source data before it enters the pipeline
Document provenance, cleaning decisions and definitions, and validate outputs against an independent source
Restrict edit access to the dataset, so values cannot be altered after loading
Keep the raw data file unchanged and perform all cleaning on a working copy
questions.explanation: (A), (C) and (D) are all genuine integrity practices, and (B) is the one that makes the others checkable — without documentation and independent validation, you cannot demonstrate that any of them worked. Integrity is a process, not a property of the image: traceability from the number on the chart back to the source record is what makes a visualisation defensible.
